steps.prompt: In how many ways can $5$ identical sweets be shared among $3$ children, if some children may get none? Try drawing the sweets as dots and the splits between children as lines.

cards.title: Stars and bars
cards.body: Share $n$ identical things among $k$ people: write the $n$ things as stars and put $k - 1$ bars between them to split them up. Every way of sharing is one row of $n + k - 1$ symbols, so the count is $\binom{n + k - 1}{k - 1}$. It also counts the solutions of $x_1 + \cdots + x_k = n$ in whole numbers $x_i \geq 0$.

cards.title: Worked example: sweets
cards.problem: In how many ways can $7$ identical sweets be shared among $3$ children, if a child may get none?

steps.text: Use $7$ stars and $2$ bars: a row of $9$ symbols.

try.prompt: How many symbols are in each row?

steps.text: Choose where the $2$ bars go: $\binom{9}{2} = 36$ ways.

try.prompt: How many ways are there to share the sweets?

cards.title: At least one each
cards.body: If everyone must get at least one, hand out one each first, then share what is left with stars and bars. For positive whole numbers, $x_1 + \cdots + x_k = n$ has $\binom{n - 1}{k - 1}$ solutions. The same trick works for "at least $2$ each".

cards.title: Worked example: positive solutions
cards.problem: How many solutions does $a + b + c + d = 10$ have in positive integers?

try.prompt: How much is left to share after that?

cards.title: The common trap: which kind of sharing?
cards.body: Stars and bars needs the things to be identical (sweets, not named people) and the boxes to be different (children, not piles). Read whether a box may be empty: $\binom{n + k - 1}{k - 1}$ allows zeros, $\binom{n - 1}{k - 1}$ doesn't.

prompts: How do you change a problem with "at least one each" into one where zeros are allowed?
